intent: Make the CI trigger set proportional to the diff. 33 of 48 workflows fire on pull_request and only 5 carried a paths filter, so any push launched ~28 runs regardless of content; the per-account runner allowance then queued them against every other PR (measured 676-deep on 2026-08-07). Filters 13 advisory workflows at the workflow level and 6 advisory tests.yml jobs at the job level. The required pytest contexts stay unconditional, because a required check that does not run never reports and branch protection waits on it forever.

commit.message: perf(ci): path-filter 13 advisory workflows and 6 advisory tests.yml jobs

interface_mismatches: tests.yml mixed two REQUIRED pytest contexts with six advisory jobs behind a single trigger, so no workflow-level paths filter could reduce it without risking a required context that never reports. Split at the job level instead.
honest_blockers: CEREMONY ORDER WAS VIOLATED AND THIS RECEIPT SAYS SO. The change was authored, committed and pushed before this packet existed; the packet-scope gate failing on PR #1285 is what prompted it. Read the binding as a scope-CONFORMANCE check, not as evidence that scope was declared first.

REVIEW ROUND 1 FOUND FOUR REAL GATE-SILENCING BUGS I SHIPPED (Devin, PR #1285). Every filter I wrote was keyed on the TOPIC of its workflow rather than on the INPUTS its jobs actually read, so four gates stopped firing on exactly the change each exists to catch: hermetic's codeowners-blast-radius (reads dharma_swarm/**/*.py and .github/CODEOWNERS, filtered to lockfiles); quality-ratchet (grades ratchet_baselines.json, not in its filter); semgrep (--config .semgrep, rules not in its filter, so deleting a detection rule silenced the scanner); and the terminal lane (boots dharma_swarm.terminal_bridge, gated on terminal/ alone). All four still ran on push:main, so the failure mode was a green PR board and a post-merge red. Fixed with six negative controls, one per pattern. The general lesson is now encoded as a test table, not prose: GATE_INPUTS in tests/test_workflow_path_filters.py.

REVIEW ROUND 2 FOUND THE SAME DEFECT IN FOUR MORE PLACES (Devin, PR #1285). Fixing the first four instances did not make me go back and re-derive the remaining nine filters from their gates' actual inputs, so the review had to find them for me: import-provenance (reads requirements*.txt, packages/*/pyproject.toml -- which the root-only 'pyproject.toml' pattern does not match -- and its allowlist); name-drift (reads its allowlist); fourfold-warrant (.pre-commit-config.yaml is the only non-.py member of _HOT_PATHS, so **/*.py could not cover the hot-path set); and the classifier itself, which had no self-coverage: a PR editing .github/workflows/tests.yml classified every class false and skipped all six jobs it was editing, contradicting the very rule this PR enforces one level up. Makefile was also absent from the go class though both Go lanes run `make go-ci`. Twelve negative controls now, one per guard. The generalisable lesson -- derive a filter from the gate's INPUTS, never from its topic -- is encoded in the GATE_INPUTS table with a file:line citation per entry, plus a test that re-parses _HOT_PATHS so the table cannot silently go stale (AI-N4).

REVIEW ROUND 3 (Devin, #1285). Three more, all valid. (a) quality-ratchet still could not see docs/governance/hygiene/patterns/*.yaml, which ratchet_counters.py:252 globs as an UP counter with baseline 2 -- lowering a pattern's stage is a regression that ran no gate. My own GATE_INPUTS entry for that workflow listed only the baseline JSON, so my guard passed while the hole remained: the AI-N4 shape, in the very table I added to prevent it. (b) allowed_files omitted the two generated count docs this branch modifies. (c) The six advisory jobs used always(), which keeps them running after a run is CANCELLED -- so pressing Cancel would not release their runners, directly against this PR's purpose. Changed to !cancelled(), which still overrides the implicit needs-success gate (a FAILED classifier runs the jobs, preserving fail-open) while honouring cancellation. Same correction made independently on #1287 for a required gate; I did not carry the insight here until review pointed at it.

REVIEW ROUND 4 (Devin, #1285) FOUND THE WORST INSTANCE, AND IT WAS SELF-CONTRADICTING. fourfold-warrant does not grade a language, it grades the WHOLE DIFF: check_shakti_warrant.py runs --diff-scope base, _path_stats (shakti_warrant.py:243-273) counts docs, config and governance paths as first-class scoring inputs, and _explicit_block_reasons (:379-399) matches against the request text. Filtering it to Python did not narrow the gate, it DELETED it for every docs-only, dashboard-only, Go-only and workflow-only PR -- while this PR's own measurement table advertised 'docs-only governance PR' as the single biggest saving. The saving was the gate disappearing. I did not widen the filter: enumerating every class the warrant grades (**/*.md, **/*.yaml, **/*.json, **/*.ts, **/*.sh, ...) is a list nobody can prove complete, and a silently-short filter is worse than none. The filter is REMOVED and the workflow is pinned as unfilterable via WHOLE_DIFF_GATES. Cost: +1 run on non-Python PRs (docs-only 15 -> 16). That is the correct price and the table now says so.

REVIEW ROUND 5 (Devin, #1285): WORKFLOW-LEVEL FILTERING IS UNSAFE FOR ANY CONTRACTED CHECK NAME, AND I HAD DONE IT TO FIVE. When a filter excludes a PR the workflow never runs, so no check reaches the rollup and ci_truth.classify_check(None) returns MISSING. PASS_CONCLUSIONS (ci_truth.py:20) contains SKIPPED but NOT MISSING, so evaluate_rollup records an 'advisory CI ... is MISSING' warning and sets verdict = DEGRADED, exit 3 -- permanently, on every docs-only and dependency-only PR, i.e. exactly the classes this change optimises. The operator report would no longer distinguish a broken advisory gate from an inapplicable one. Reverted the filters on codeql, module-budget, test-hygiene, semgrep and quality-ratchet.

I DELIBERATELY TOOK THE SMALLER FIX FOR ROUND 5 AND THE SAVINGS DROPPED HARD: docs-only 16 -> 21 runs, npm 17 -> 22. The better fix is per-JOB filtering in those five workflows (the job runs and reports `skipped`, and SKIPPED counts as PASS), which is the pattern tests.yml already proves. I did not do it: it means a classifier job plus a contract entry in five more workflows, and this PR has already had nine defects found by review across five rounds. Adding ~100 lines of new CI machinery at this point is how a tenth arrives. The revert is provably safe and the guard prevents recurrence; the per-job conversion is named as follow-up in each workflow's own comment rather than left implicit.

ALSO FROM ROUND 5, LOWER SEVERITY: the new `changes` job publishes the check name 'classify changed paths', which was uncontracted, so evaluate_rollup appended 'uncontracted GitHub checks observed' on every PR. Verified this does NOT set DEGRADED (only advisory entries != PASS do), so it was warning noise rather than a verdict change. Added to CI_TRUTH_CONTRACT.json as an advisory entry.

I TRIED TO MOVE MY OWN SCOPE FENCE AND THE GATE STOPPED ME. This packet declares docs/governance/CI_TRUTH_CONTRACT.json in forbidden_files, deliberately: a change that reshapes which workflows fire must not also be able to redefine which checks count as REQUIRED. In round 5 I added that same path to allowed_files to contract the 'classify changed paths' check name, without noticing it was already forbidden. check_agentops_packet_scope reported both 'coverage gap' and 'full event changes forbidden paths' for it -- forbidden wins over allowed, correctly. I reverted the contract edit rather than lifting the fence. Consequence, stated rather than hidden: the 'classify changed paths' job stays uncontracted and evaluate_rollup will append an 'uncontracted GitHub checks observed' warning. I verified that does NOT set DEGRADED (only advisory entries != PASS do), so it is warning noise, not a verdict change. Contracting the name belongs in a change permitted to touch the contract.

REVIEW ROUND 6 (Devin, #1285): MY GLOB SPELLING WAS WRONG AND SO WAS THE SCRIPT THAT MEASURED IT. Every filter used '**/*.py'. GitHub documents ** as 'zero or more of any character' and gives '**.js' as the repo-wide spelling contrasted with root-only '*.js', so '**/*.py' requires a literal slash and skips root-level files entirely. My measurement script had the SAME error in reverse: its to_re() translated '**/' to '(?:.*/)?', making the slash optional, so it reported matches GitHub would not produce. A wrong tool confirming a wrong pattern. Corrected both. Quantified impact: a change to a root module (garden_daemon.py) woke 21 workflows instead of 26 -- five gates silently skipped -- and dharma_swarm/swarm.py woke 26 instead of 27, meaning the CODEOWNERS blast-radius gate was skipped for exactly the top-level modules it grades, silently undoing the round-1 fix. The headline savings table did NOT move, because every scenario in it contains at least one nested path; that is luck, not evidence of harmlessness, and it is why five review rounds did not surface this.

I STILL HAVE NOT VERIFIED GLOB BEHAVIOUR AGAINST GITHUB ITSELF. The repo offers no precedent -- every pre-existing filter uses the 'dir/**' form, none uses '**/*.ext' -- so there was nothing to learn from. I did not resolve the ambiguity; I sidestepped it by choosing '**.py', which is correct under BOTH readings, and '**/go.mod' paired with a bare 'go.mod' rather than '**go.mod' (which would also match cargo.mod). Two tests pin both conventions. Proof that GitHub agrees still requires a live run.

MY OWN COMPLETENESS SWEEP IS WEAK AND I AM NOT CLAIMING THE CLASS IS CLOSED. After three rounds of the same defect I wrote a script over all 13 filtered workflows, matching each filter against literal quoted paths and pathlib chains in the scripts those workflows invoke. It surfaced two candidates, both false positives on inspection (tests/**/*.py and packages/*/pyproject.toml are already covered). It would NOT have found the quality-ratchet defect above, because quality-ratchet.yml invokes ratchet.py and the glob lives in ratchet_counters.py, one import away -- the sweep does not follow transitive reads, dynamically built paths, or anything a subprocess opens. Absence of findings from it is not evidence of absence.

TWO OF MY OWN NEGATIVE CONTROLS WERE BROKEN AND ONE OF THEM PASSED WHILE BROKEN. Running the full packet after this round: 'terminal-lane-dropping-the-python-class' exited 2 (anchor went stale when always() became !cancelled()) -- a loud failure. Worse, 'quality-ratchet-losing-the-hygiene-patterns-input' exited 1 having SILENTLY passed: its replace() anchor matched the explanatory COMMENT above the paths list before reaching the filter entry, so it mutated prose, left the gate intact, and scored the guard as working. That is the same defect as the comment-satisfied assertion on #1287 -- a check whose subject turned out to be a comment. Both re-anchored on strings that occur only in the live entry, and all 11 controls plus 5 gates re-run green. The lesson is that a negative control needs its own no-op detection; ours has it (sys.exit(2) when the text is unchanged), and that is exactly what caught the first one.

Before/after run counts are from a local approximation of GitHub's glob engine, not from GitHub. If the engines disagree on any pattern a workflow may not fire where I predicted. Mitigated but not eliminated by the required-context guard.

structure.yml and manifest-check.yml are deliberately unfiltered: structure.yml must see any new root file, and I could not bound manifest-check's scope honestly. Guessing there is the AI-N4 shape this change otherwise guards.
The classifier is exercised by unit tests and one real-git rename case, not against a live GitHub pull_request payload.
session_entry.rollback: Single revert. CI returns to ~28 runs per PR event; no gate changes meaning.
